mainTopic: Where we learn that a person (אדם המזיק) pays for damage even when it was unintentional or by accident, and רבה's case of a stone falling from someone's lap, compared across several areas of halacha.
overview: The גמרא asks for the source of the rule that a person pays for damage even when he did not mean to cause it. חזקיה learns it from the extra word 'תחת' in 'פצע תחת פצע,' which teaches both this rule and payment for צער. רבה then gives a series of cases: a stone that falls from someone's lap when he did not know it was there, a stone he knew about but forgot, and a stone he threw farther than he planned. In each case he compares נזקין, the ארבעה דברים, שבת, גלות, and freeing an עבד. For the עבד, the answer always depends on a מחלוקת between רבן שמעון בן גמליאל and the רבנן about a master who was a doctor. Next, רבה rules on a vessel thrown off a roof. Someone who smashes it on the way down is exempt, because it was 'already broken.' A thrower whose vessel was protected by cushions when he threw it is also exempt, even if the cushions are removed afterward. Finally, רבה says that a child thrown off a roof and caught on a sword depends on a מחלוקת between רבי יהודה בן בתירא and the רבנן. The גמרא begins quoting that ברייתא, and it continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Asking for the source
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks where we learn that a person who causes damage pays even when he did not mean to.
steps.simpleTranslation: From where do we know these things?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up the next move: it asks for a source in the תורה for the rule just discussed, that a person is liable for damage even without intent.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule itself is already accepted. The question is only about which פסוק it comes from, so the answer will be a source, not a new law.

keyTerms.meaning: From where do we know these things? (asking for a source)

phrases.english: From where are these matters derived?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a search for the source of a rule taught just before this point.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The פסוק that makes a person liable for unintentional and accidental damage.

steps.title: חזקיה learns it from 'wound for wound'
steps.stepSummary: חזקיה, together with the teaching of his בית מדרש, learns from 'פצע תחת פצע' that unintentional and accidental damage are treated like deliberate damage.
steps.simpleTranslation: חזקיה said, and the school of חזקיה taught the same: the פסוק says 'a wound for a wound.' This makes him liable for a mistake the same as on purpose, and for an accident the same as willingly.
steps.whatsHappening: חזקיה answers the question by pointing to the פסוק 'פצע תחת פצע'. He reads it as teaching that a person pays even for damage done by mistake or by accident.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The idea is that a wound is a wound no matter how it happened. So the person who caused it pays whether it was שוגג or אונס, the same as if it was מזיד or done willingly.

keyTerms.meaning: Done by mistake, without meaning to

phrases.english: Ḥizkiyya says,
and similarly, the school of Ḥizkiyya taught:
The verse states: “Wound for wound” —
to render him liable for the unintentional as for the intentional,
and for an accident as for a willing act.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר חִזְקִיָּה, וְכֵן תָּנָא דְּבֵי חִזְקִיָּה, אָמַר קְרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the source question of step 1.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The פסוק 'פצע תחת פצע' teaches liability for שוגג like מזיד and for אונס like רצון.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is the basis for the well-known rule that אדם מועד לעולם: a person always pays for the damage he causes.

steps.title: That verse is needed for something else
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects that 'פצע תחת פצע' is already needed to teach payment for צער even where נזק is paid.
steps.simpleTranslation: But this פסוק is needed to teach that he pays for pain even where he pays for damage!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges חזקיה: the פסוק is already being used for a different lesson, so how can it also teach his point?
steps.deeperAnalysis: There is a general rule that a פסוק already used for one lesson cannot simply be taken for another. 'פצע תחת פצע' is already the source that someone who pays נזק must also pay צער, so it seems to be 'used up'.

keyTerms.meaning: It is needed for (a different lesson)
Pain; one of the payments for injuring a person
Damage; the loss in value from the injury

phrases.english: But this verse is needed
to require payment for pain even where he pays for damage!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the source given in step 2.
steps.kashyaTarget: חזקיה's use of 'פצע תחת פצע' as the source for liability in שוגג and אונס.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The פסוק is already used to teach צער במקום נזק, so it is not free to teach another rule.

steps.title: The word 'תחת' teaches two lessons
steps.stepSummary: Answer: the פסוק could have said 'פצע בפצע'. The wording 'תחת' shows it teaches both lessons.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, let the פסוק write 'פצע בפצע'. Why does it say 'תחת פצע'? Learn two things from it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the פסוק is worded with extra length on purpose. That extra wording lets it teach both צער and liability for mistakes and accidents.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the only point were צער, a shorter wording would have been enough. The choice of 'תחת' signals an extra lesson. So חזקיה's teaching and the צער teaching both come from this one פסוק.

keyTerms.meaning: If so (if the פסוק taught only that)

phrases.english: If so, let the verse write: “Wound by wound”;
what is meant by “for a wound”?
Conclude from it two lessons.

steps.terutzResolutionType: Extra wording in the פסוק allows a second lesson.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The פסוק teaches only צער במקום נזק.
steps.terutzMaskana: Because of the word 'תחת', the פסוק teaches both צער במקום נזק and liability for שוגג and אונס.
steps.whatToRemember: 'פצע תחת פצע' teaches two things: a person pays צער along with נזק, and a person pays for damage even by mistake or accident.

steps.title: רבה's case of the stone in his lap
steps.stepSummary: רבה: a stone he did not know about falls from a man's lap when he stands. He pays נזקין, is exempt from the ארבעה דברים, is not liable for שבת, and is exempt from גלות.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה said: A stone was lying in a person's lap and he did not know about it. He stood up and it fell. For damages he is liable. For the four payments he is exempt. For שבת, the תורה forbade only planned work. For exile he is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה gives one event, a stone falling from someone's lap without his knowledge, and shows how it comes out in different areas of halacha.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For plain damage (נזק) he pays, because of the rule just learned that a person pays even for accidents. But for the extra payments (ארבעה דברים), for שבת (which needs מלאכת מחשבת), and for גלות, an act this unaware does not make him liable.

keyTerms.meaning: The four extra payments: צער, ריפוי, שבת, בושת
Planned, intended work; what is forbidden on שבת
Exile to an עיר מקלט for killing by mistake

phrases.english: Rabba says:
If there was a stone lying in his lap
and he was unaware of it,
and he arose and it fell;
with regard to damages, he is liable;
with regard to the four types of payment, he is exempt;
phrases.notes: These are the four payments besides נזק: pain, medical costs, lost work time, and embarrassment.

phrases.english: with regard to Shabbat —
the Torah prohibited only planned labor,
with regard to exile, he is exempt;

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבָּה: הָיְתָה אֶבֶן מוּנַּחַת לוֹ בְּחֵיקוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies the rule of liability for accidents to a case and contrasts it with other areas of halacha.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An unaware act (the stone in his lap) makes him liable for נזק only. He is exempt from the ארבעה דברים, not liable for שבת, and exempt from גלות.
steps.confusionAlert: He is not exempt from everything. He still pays the basic נזק. Only the other areas need more awareness than this.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that a person's liability for נזק is stricter than almost any other area of halacha.

steps.title: For freeing a slave, it depends on a dispute
steps.stepSummary: רבה adds that whether a slave hurt by the falling stone goes free depends on a מחלוקת between רבן שמעון בן גמליאל and the רבנן.
steps.simpleTranslation: Regarding a slave, it is the dispute of רבן שמעון בן גמליאל and the רבנן.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה continues his list with the case of an עבד who loses an eye or tooth from the stone. He says this is not clear-cut, because it depends on an existing מחלוקת.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Unlike the earlier areas, here רבה does not give one answer. He ties the case to a known dispute about whether a master's unintended injury frees the slave. The next step brings that dispute.

keyTerms.meaning: A slave; one who goes free if his master knocks out his eye or tooth

phrases.english: with regard to a slave —
phrases.notes: He means a slave whose eye or tooth was destroyed by the falling stone, which normally sets a slave free.

phrases.aramaic: פְּלוּגְתָּא דְּרַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל וְרַבָּנַן.
phrases.english: it is the dispute between Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and the Rabbis.

steps.triggerLanguage: לְעִנְיַן עֶבֶד – פְּלוּגְתָּא דְּרַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל וְרַבָּנַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues רבה's list with the last area, the עבד.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Whether the עבד goes free in the stone case depends on the מחלוקת of רבן שמעון בן גמליאל and the רבנן.

steps.title: The ברייתא about the master who was a doctor
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא: a master who was a doctor, asked by his slave to treat his eye or tooth, accidentally blinded the eye or knocked out the tooth. The slave 'mocked the master' and goes free.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it is taught: If the master was a doctor and the slave said to him 'paint my eye' and he blinded it, or 'scrape my tooth' and he knocked it out, the slave has mocked the master and goes free.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the ברייתא where the dispute rabbis רבה mentioned is found. The first opinion in it says the slave goes free even though the master did not mean to hurt him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The master was trying to help, yet the slave still goes free. This first opinion treats unintended injury as enough to free an עבד, like an unaware act. The other side of the dispute, רבן שמעון בן גמליאל, comes next in the text.

keyTerms.meaning: He mocked (got the better of) the master

phrases.english: As it is taught: If his master was a doctor,
and the slave said to him: “Paint my eye,” and he blinded it;
or “Scrape my tooth for me,” and he knocked it out —
the slave has mocked the master, and he goes out to freedom.
phrases.notes: The slave asked for help and ended up free, so he 'got the better' of his master.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings the ברייתא that contains the מחלוקת mentioned in step 6.
steps.raayaObject: That there is a מחלוקת about whether an unintended injury frees an עבד.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא about the master who was a doctor and blinded his slave's eye or knocked out his tooth.

steps.title: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל: the master must intend to destroy
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא ends with רבן שמעון בן גמליאל, who reads the word וְשִׁחֲתָהּ to mean the slave goes free only if the master meant to destroy the eye or tooth.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says: the פסוק says 'and destroys it.' The slave goes free only when the master intends to destroy it.
steps.whatsHappening: This finishes the ברייתא from the last step. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל disagrees with the רבנן and says the doctor-master's slave does not go free.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The רבנן said the slave goes free even though the master was trying to heal him. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל learns from the word וְשִׁחֲתָהּ that the master must mean to destroy the eye or tooth. This shows where רבה's falling-stone case comes from: by the רבנן the slave goes free, but by רבן שמעון בן גמליאל he does not.

keyTerms.meaning: "And destroys it": a word from the פסוק about a master hurting his slave's eye
He intends or means to do it

steps.whatToRemember: By the רבנן, a slave goes free even if the injury was unintended. By רבן שמעון בן גמליאל, he goes free only if the master meant to destroy the limb.

phrases.english: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says:
"And destroys it" means:
only when he intends to destroy it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the ברייתא quoted in step 7 by giving the opposing view.
steps.raayaObject: רבה's claim in step 6 that the slave in the falling-stone case depends on a מחלוקת.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא of the doctor-master: the רבנן free the slave, and רבן שמעון בן גמליאל requires intent to destroy.

steps.title: He knew about the stone but forgot it
steps.stepSummary: רבה's next case: he once knew about the stone, then forgot it. He is liable for נזקין and גלות, and exempt from ארבעה דברים and שבת. The slave depends on the מחלוקת.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he knew about the stone, forgot it, stood up, and it fell: for damages he is liable. For the four payments he is exempt. For exile he is liable, because the פסוק says 'בשגגה,' which implies he once had knowledge, and here he did have knowledge. For שבת he is exempt. For a slave, it depends on the argument between רבן שמעון בן גמליאל and the רבנן.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה changes his case a little: now the man had known about the stone before he forgot it. He goes through the same list of laws again.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The big change is גלות. In step 5, where he never knew about the stone, he was exempt. Now he is liable, because שגגה means a mistake by someone who once knew. Everything else stays the same as in step 5.

keyTerms.meaning: By mistake: the word the Torah uses for an accidental killer who goes to exile
Which implies; we can learn from this
Exile to a city of refuge for an accidental killer

steps.confusionAlert: Don't think forgetting makes him less responsible than never knowing. For גלות it's the opposite: a שוגג is someone who knew and forgot, so here he is liable, while in step 5 he was exempt.

phrases.english: If he knew about it and then forgot it,
and he stood up and it fell;
regarding damages, he is liable.
Regarding the four payments, he is exempt.
Regarding exile, he is liable,
since the פסוק says: "by mistake":
which implies that he had knowledge at some point,
and here he did have knowledge.
Regarding שבת, he is exempt.
Regarding a slave, it is the argument
of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and the Rabbis.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to רבה's list from step 5 with a slightly changed case.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Known-then-forgotten stone: liable for נזקין and גלות; exempt from ארבעה דברים and שבת; the slave depends on the מחלוקת.

steps.title: He meant to throw two אמות but threw four
steps.stepSummary: He threw on purpose, but the stone went farther than he planned. He is liable for נזקין. He is exempt from ארבעה דברים and שבת. The פסוק אשר לא צדה covers גלות. The slave depends on the מחלוקת.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he meant to throw two and threw four: for damages he is liable. For the four payments he is exempt. For שבת, we need a planned act. For exile, the Torah said 'אשר לא צדה,' which excludes one who meant to throw two and threw four. For a slave, it depends on the argument between רבן שמעון בן גמליאל and the רבנן.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה gives a new case: now the throw was on purpose, but it went too far. He again goes through each area of law.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There is no שבת liability. Throwing four אמות in a public area is a forbidden מלאכה, but he only planned two, so it wasn't a planned מלאכה. For גלות, אשר לא צדה shows he is not treated as a deliberate killer, because he never aimed to kill. So he goes to גלות.

keyTerms.meaning: A planned, thought-out act: what you need to be liable on שבת
"Who did not lie in wait": the פסוק about an accidental killer
To exclude, or to single out, a certain case
"The Merciful One": a name for ה׳ as the Giver of the Torah

phrases.english: If he intended to throw it two,
phrases.notes: Two אמות. The גמרא leaves out the word, and four אמות is the distance that matters for throwing on שבת.

phrases.english: but he threw it four;
regarding damages, he is liable.
Regarding the four payments, he is exempt.
Regarding שבת, we require a planned act.

phrases.aramaic: לְעִנְיַן גָּלוּת – ״אֲשֶׁר לֹא צָדָה״ אָמַר רַחֲמָנָא,
phrases.english: Regarding exile, the Torah said: "who did not lie in wait",
to exclude one who intended to throw two
and threw four.
Regarding a slave, it is the argument
of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and the Rabbis.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from a stone that fell by itself to a stone thrown on purpose that went too far.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Meant two, threw four: liable for נזקין; exempt from ארבעה דברים and שבת (no planned act); אשר לא צדה shows he is not a deliberate killer, so he goes to גלות; the slave depends on the מחלוקת.

steps.title: He meant to throw four אמות but threw eight
steps.stepSummary: Same as the last case, except for שבת. He is liable only if he said, 'wherever it lands is fine.'
steps.simpleTranslation: If he meant to throw four and threw eight: for damages he is liable. For the four payments he is exempt. For שבת, if he said 'wherever you want, land,' then yes, he is liable; if not, no. For exile, 'אשר לא צדה' excludes one who meant to throw four and threw eight. For a slave, it depends on the argument between רבן שמעון בן גמליאל and the רבנן.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה gives his last case: now he planned a full four אמות, but it flew eight. Only the שבת ruling changes.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He did plan a real four-אמה throw, so on שבת it depends on what he had in mind. If any landing spot was fine with him, he did what he planned and is liable. If he had a set target four אמות away, the stone didn't do what he planned, so he is exempt.

keyTerms.meaning: "Wherever you want, land": he doesn't care where the stone lands

steps.whatToRemember: The cases build step by step. Not knowing about the stone at all means no גלות. Knowing and forgetting, or throwing farther than planned, means גלות. For שבת, the act must match what he planned. For the slave, every case depends on the מחלוקת between רבן שמעון בן גמליאל and the רבנן.

phrases.english: If he intended to throw it four,
but he threw it eight;
regarding damages, he is liable.
Regarding the four payments, he is exempt.
Regarding שבת: if he says,
"Wherever you want, land," then yes, he is liable;
phrases.notes: He means he is talking to the stone. Any spot past four אמות is fine with him.

phrases.english: if not, then he is not liable.
Regarding exile: "who did not lie in wait",
to exclude one who intended to throw four
and threw eight.
Regarding a slave, it is the argument
of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and the Rabbis.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Repeats the throwing case with a planned four-אמה throw, which changes only the שבת ruling.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Meant four, threw eight: liable for נזקין; exempt from ארבעה דברים; for שבת, liable only if he didn't care where it landed; גלות as before; the slave depends on the מחלוקת.

steps.title: Breaking a vessel that was already falling to its doom
steps.stepSummary: רבה rules that if someone throws a vessel off a roof and another person smashes it with a stick on the way down, the one with the stick is exempt. The vessel was already 'broken.'
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבה said: If someone threw a vessel from the top of a roof, and another person came and broke it with a stick, he is exempt. Why? He broke a vessel that was already broken.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה gives a new ruling about a vessel thrown off a roof that someone else smashes before it lands. The person who smashed it does not have to pay.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once the vessel was thrown, it was certain to shatter when it hit the ground. So we treat it as already broken. The second person only 'broke a broken thing,' and that damaged nothing of value.
steps.confusionAlert: This ruling only covers the second person, the one with the stick. רבה is not saying the first person, who threw the vessel, is exempt. The thrower is the one who doomed the vessel.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up the main idea of this group of rulings: once an object is doomed by an earlier act, we treat it as already destroyed.

phrases.english: And Rabba said:
If one threw a vessel from the top of the roof,
and another came and broke it with a stick, he is exempt.
phrases.notes: The one who is exempt here is the second person, the one who swung the stick.

phrases.english: What is the reason?
He broke a broken vessel.
phrases.notes: Once it was thrown, it was going to smash anyway, so we treat it as already broken.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַבָּה: זָרַק כְּלִי מֵרֹאשׁ הַגָּג
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Another ruling from רבה. It follows his earlier rulings about a thrown stone, but now the topic is damaging something that was already doomed.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Someone who smashes a vessel that is already falling to certain destruction is exempt, because it is treated as already broken.

steps.title: Cushions removed after the vessel was thrown
steps.stepSummary: רבה rules that if someone throws a vessel onto cushions and the cushions are then removed, the thrower is exempt. This is true whether someone else removed them or the thrower did. When he threw it, his throw could not break it.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבה said: If someone threw a vessel from the top of a roof, and there were cushions or blankets under it, and another person came and removed them, or he himself rushed ahead and removed them, he is exempt. Why? At the moment he threw it, the force of his throw was blocked.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה gives the opposite kind of case. This time the vessel was safe when it was thrown, because cushions were waiting below. The cushions were removed only afterward, and the thrower does not pay.
steps.deeperAnalysis: We judge the thrower by what his throw could do at the moment he threw. Back then, the cushions 'cut off his arrows,' so his throw had no power to break the vessel. Removing the cushions later is a separate act, not part of the throw.

keyTerms.meaning: at the time he threw it
his arrows (the force of his throw)

steps.confusionAlert: This is true even when the thrower himself removed the cushions. The point is that the throw itself was harmless. The later removal does not count as part of the throw.
steps.whyThisMatters: Together with the last step, this shows that רבה looks at the moment of the act: was the object already doomed, or was it still safe?

phrases.english: And Rabba said:
If one threw a vessel from the top of the roof,
and there were cushions or blankets beneath it;
another came and removed them,
or he himself went ahead and removed them, he is exempt.
phrases.notes: The word in square brackets, הוּא ("he"), is part of the corrected wording; some versions don't have it.

phrases.english: What is the reason?
At the time that he threw it,
his arrows were cut off.
phrases.notes: A picture of an arrow being blocked: the cushions meant his throw had no power to break anything.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַבָּה: זָרַק כְּלִי מֵרֹאשׁ הַגָּג, וְהָיוּ תַּחְתָּיו כָּרִים אוֹ כְסָתוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The opposite case of Step 12. There the vessel was already doomed when it was thrown; here it was safe when it was thrown.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If a thrown vessel was protected when it was thrown, the thrower is exempt even if the protection is removed later, even by himself.

steps.title: A child thrown off a roof and caught on a sword
steps.stepSummary: רבה says that if someone throws a child off a roof and another person catches the child on a sword, who is liable depends on a מחלוקת between רבי יהודה בן בתירא and the רבנן.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבה said: If someone threw a child from the top of a roof, and another person came and caught him on a sword, this depends on the מחלוקת between רבי יהודה בן בתירא and the רבנן.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה brings the same 'already doomed' idea to a case of killing a person. He does not give a ruling; he says it depends on an earlier argument, and this sets up the ברייתא that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The child was going to die from the fall, so is he treated as already 'dead' when the sword kills him? A vessel can be called 'already broken,' but with a human life the answer is not simple. So רבה ties it to a known מחלוקת about killing someone who is already dying.

phrases.english: And Rabba said:
If one threw a child from the top of the roof,
and another came and caught him on a sword,

phrases.aramaic: פְּלוּגְתָּא דְּרַבִּי יְהוּדָה בֶּן בְּתֵירָא וְרַבָּנַן.
phrases.english: it is the dispute of Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira and the Rabbis.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַבָּה: זָרַק תִּינוֹק מֵרֹאשׁ הַגָּג
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves the 'already doomed' idea from Step 12 from objects to a human life, where the answer depends on a מחלוקת.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Who is liable when someone kills a child already falling to his death depends on the מחלוקת between רבי יהודה בן בתירא and the רבנן.

steps.title: The ברייתא of ten people hitting with ten sticks begins
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא begins quoting the ברייתא behind the מחלוקת: ten people hit someone with ten sticks, at the same time or one after another. The amud ends at 'all of them,' and the ruling continues on the next amud.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it was taught in a ברייתא: If ten people hit him with ten sticks, whether at the same time or one after the other, all of them...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is quoting the source of the מחלוקת רבה just mentioned. The amud ends in the middle of the ברייתא's sentence; the ruling comes on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא describes many people adding blows to the same victim. The question is whether a later hitter, who struck someone already badly beaten, counts as a killer. That is the same kind of question as the sword hitting a child who was already falling to his death.

phrases.english: As it was taught in a baraita:

phrases.aramaic: הִכּוּהוּ עֲשָׂרָה בְּנֵי אָדָם בַּעֲשָׂרָה מַקְלוֹת –
phrases.english: If ten people hit him with ten sticks,
phrases.notes: 'Him' is a victim who died from the beating.

phrases.aramaic: בֵּין בְּבַת אַחַת בֵּין בָּזֶה אַחַר זֶה, כּוּלָּן
phrases.english: whether at the same time or one after the other, all of them...

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּתַנְיָא: הִכּוּהוּ עֲשָׂרָה בְּנֵי אָדָם בַּעֲשָׂרָה מַקְלוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Quotes the ברייתא that Step 14 pointed to as the source of the מחלוקת.
steps.raayaObject: רבה's claim that the case of the child on the sword depends on a known מחלוקת.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא of ten people hitting a victim with ten sticks, at the same time or one after another.
